title: Vientiane
capsule: The Kingdom of Vientiane (ວຽງຈັນ, Viang Chan) emerged in 1707 as an independent polity when the Lan Xang kingdom split into three successor states — Luang Phrabang, Vientiane, and Champasak — following a succession dispute. Situated on a bend of the Mekong, Vientiane was the most commercially active of the three, benefiting from overland trade routes connecting China and the Vietnamese coast to the Thai Gulf. The kingdom oscillated between Siamese and Burmese influence and was repeatedly pressured to acknowledge Siamese suzerainty from Bangkok. In 1826–1828, King Anouvong (Chao Anou) launched a failed uprising against Siam; the Siamese army responded by comprehensively destroying Vientiane in 1828 and deporting much of the population to the right bank of the Mekong, effectively extinguishing the kingdom.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Core territory along the middle Mekong is well documented; hinterland boundaries with Luang Phrabang and Champasak were fluid and are not precisely mapped in surviving Lao or Siamese sources.
